entry.title: 'Politics-proof' investment: Proposed Andhra law offers a template
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / 'Politics-proof' investment: Proposed Andhra law offers a template'Politics-proof' investment: Proposed Andhra law offers a template

Andhra Pradesh's investment protection law can provide policy stability and shield investors from arbitrary decisions by successive governments

premium

N Chandrababu Naidu, Chief Minister, Andhra Pradesh (Photo: PTI)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 17 2026 | 11:43 PM ISTThe Andhra Pradesh government under N Chandrababu Naidu has offered states a progressive blueprint to attract and secure investors at a time when private-sector investment, Indian or foreign, has been thin on the ground. The Investment Protection Bill, to be introduced in the upcoming Assembly session, reflects the economic cost the state has paid due to the political rivalry of successive regimes. Prominent among them is the infamous “three capitals plan” of 2019, under which the YSR Congress Party government in the state decided to scrap the plan of the previous government, whose chief minister was, again, Mr Naidu, to establish a new capital, Amaravati, in the newly bifurcated state. Instead, the state was to have three separate capitals  — legislative, executive and judicial  — all located miles apart from one another. This plan reneged on the previous government’s commitment to compensate farmers who surrendered land for the single greenfield capital. Legal battles and parliamentary intervention sorted out the matter only in September 2026. The same YSR Congress regime also scrapped long-term power-purchase agreements in renewable energy with retrospective effect, an issue that worked its way through the courts till 2022. The law concerned shields investment by ensuring that future governments cannot arbitrarily cancel or alter valid commitments. To this end, the law covers land allotment, water pricing, fiscal and non-fiscal incentives, infrastructure support and regulatory approvals. Significantly, the state also plans to introduce an escrow account to guarantee the timely delivery of industrial incentives, though it is unclear how this will function since the law is still in the drafting stage. Announced at the 31st Confederation of Indian Industry Partnership Summit in Visakhapatnam, the state government is seeking broader support from New Delhi for a National Investment Protection Act. The Concurrent List of the Constitution allows states to enact legislation of this nature but neither the states nor the Centre has such laws in place.  The chronic variability of policymaking under different political administrations suggests that states hoping to attract investment would do well to follow Andhra Pradesh’s example rather than wait for a model national law. In West Bengal, for example, the Trinamool Congress government’s arbitrary decisions to review compensation for land losers in the Tata-Nano project or the cancellation, with retrospective effect, of three decades of industrial commitments, subsidies, and other concessions played stellar roles in the further flight of industry.  The major issue, perhaps, is how far successive governments will genuinely honour the letter and spirit of such a law. Inasmuch as all laws are subject to legal challenges, the risk of investors being subjected to lengthy lawsuits by successor regimes  — a major pain point  — remains. This is a key reason India’s key economic partners, for example, are demanding a one-year window for the exhaustion of legal remedies in arbitration contracts under bilateral-investment treaties rather than the government’s reported offer of three years. Though a stable investment environment can only be as “politics-proof” as the politicians will allow, an investment-protection law will offer a degree of predictability that has been elusive in India’s economic landscape.     Topics : N Chandrababu Naidu Andhra Pradesh Investment Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: India's lower health spending burden still masks gaps in public care
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / India's lower health spending burden still masks gaps in public careIndia's lower health spending burden still masks gaps in public care

Pharmaceuticals accounted for 30.2 per cent of current health expenditure, while outpatient curative care accounted for 19.3 per cent

premium

Private hospitals accounted for around 31.9 per cent of current health expenditure, almost twice the 15.9 per cent spent through government hospitals (Photo: AdobeStock)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 17 2026 | 11:50 PM ISTThe latest estimates of the National Health Accounts (NHA) show India’s financing for health care has become less dependent on households, but this should not be mistaken for adequate public investment or universal financial protection. The share of out-of-pocket expenditure (OOPE) in total health spending indeed declined from 64.2 per cent in 2013-14 to 42.7 per cent in 2023-24. Over the same period, the government’s share rose from 28.6 per cent to 43.5 per cent. Government health expenditure increased to ₹4.14 trillion, nearly three times its level a decade earlier. These are significant shifts. But the increase is in nominal terms; more importantly, government health expenditure was only 1.43 per cent of gross domestic product in 2023-24, as against the National Health Policy 2017 target of 2.5 per cent by 2025. The target remains unmet.  At the same time, a lower OOPE share does not mean that households are no longer bearing a burden. Per capita OOPE rose from ₹2,767 in 2022-23 to ₹2,901 in 2023-24. The decline in the share must, therefore, be read alongside the absolute amount and the continuing risk of households incurring high costs when they need treatment. Insurance coverage also deserves attention in this context. The latest National Family Health Survey-6 (NFHS-6) fact sheet reports that 60.2 per cent of households had at least one usual member covered by a health-insurance or financing scheme in 2023-24, up from 41 per cent in NFHS-5. This is encouraging, but the indicator is household-based: It does not mean that 60.2 per cent of individuals have comprehensive insurance. The NHA estimates record ₹97,167 crore in private health-insurance expenditure and ₹33,385 crore under government-financed insurance schemes in 2023-24. The Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) provides up to ₹5 lakh per family for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation, but insurance-led protection does not automatically cover the costs of outpatient consultations, medicines and diagnostics.  The composition of health care spending points to why public provision remains central. Pharmaceuticals accounted for 30.2 per cent of current health expenditure, while outpatient curative care accounted for 19.3 per cent. These are expenses that can recur and weigh heavily on households. Private hospitals accounted for around 31.9 per cent of current health expenditure, almost twice the 15.9 per cent spent through government hospitals. Expanding insurance without adequate public facilities risks financing treatment in a system where private providers remain a bigger part of delivery. The Centre cannot meet this challenge alone and states accounted for about 68 per cent of government health expenditure in 2023-24. However, their fiscal capacity and health infrastructure vary considerably. Government spending is directed substantially towards primary care, which accounts for around 51 per cent of its current health expenditure, as it should. However, this must translate into functioning facilities, adequately staffed centres, reliable supplies of medicines, diagnostic services, and accessible outpatient care. The NHA numbers mark genuine progress in the way health care is financed. But a falling OOPE share needs to be seen in the overall context. The priority must be to raise public-health spending towards the stated target while strengthening primary care and public hospitals.     Topics : healthcare Expenditure Health Insurance Ayushman Bharat Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: MTNL-BSNL merger needs a fresh review as India's telecom market evolves
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / MTNL-BSNL merger needs a fresh review as India's telecom market evolvesMTNL-BSNL merger needs a fresh review as India's telecom market evolves

MTNL, which has a rich land bank, should not be viewed only as a real-estate play. The land monetisation should lead to a strong merged entity in a competitive landscape

premium

Photo: Shutterstock

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 16 2026 | 11:18 PM ISTMahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd (MTNL), once a valued state-owned telecom-service company, has been in the news for the sale of its land assets. Recently, the Inter-Ministerial Group (IMG) on Asset Monetisation recommended for Cabinet approval monetising a fresh tranche of the telco’s surplus land and building assets valued at ₹1,100 crore. While monetising land assets has been an ongoing initiative aimed at reducing the piled up debt of MTNL, which offers services in Delhi and Mumbai, the government must provide clarity on the telco’s future and that of its subscribers. With landline or wireline teledensity (active connections per 100 people) in India at just 3.4 per cent, there’s room for growth in that segment for both calls and the broadband network. In fact, over the past one year or so, there’s been a significant uptick in fixed-phone subscriber numbers, driven by the fibre-to-the-home (FTTH) broadband rollout and growth on the enterprise side. Perhaps, MTNL can still play a constructive role in this space in a timebound manner.  MTNL, which continues to be a listed entity on the stock exchanges, has over the years witnessed erosion in its subscriber base and churn due to its indifferent service quality along with a lack of manpower and resources amid intense competition from the private sector. Even as MTNL is being operated by the unlisted Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd (BSNL) since January 2025 under a service agreement, the much-anticipated merger between the two state-owned telcos was put on hold a few years ago because of MTNL’s financial liabilities, which are estimated at over ₹40,000 crore. While MTNL operates only in Delhi and Mumbai, BSNL is a pan-Indian service provider.  The latest data from the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (Trai) shows MTNL had only a 2.09 per cent market share in landline-phone connections as of end September. In the same segment, Reliance Jio is on top with 33.06 per cent, followed by Bharti Airtel at 25.46 per cent, Tata Tele at 23.07 per cent, BSNL at 13.67 per cent, Vodafone Idea at 1.57 per cent, and other smaller players holding the remaining market share. The number of landline subscribers in the country increased to 48.74 million at the end of September, from 48.45 million a month earlier, showing a monthly growth rate of 0.60 per cent. In the wireless segment, MTNL is at a 0.01 per cent market share. Jio leads in wireless numbers too with a market share of 39.32 per cent and Bharti Airtel is a close second at 38.02 per cent, while Vodafone Idea is at 15.39 per cent and BSNL at 7.25 per cent. India’s wireless teledensity is estimated at 92.12 per cent.  Since telecom is classified as a strategic sector, the government may not be willing to privatise MTNL. Against that backdrop, the proposal to merge MTNL and BSNL, which has shown signs of operational recovery, though still in losses, should be revived with a definite road map rather than continuing with a service agreement between the two companies, which were telecom heavyweights in the past. MTNL, which has a rich land bank, should not be viewed only as a real-estate play. The land monetisation should lead to a strong merged entity in a competitive landscape.     Topics : Business Standard Editorial Comment BS Opinion Telecom industry MTNL

entry.title: India needs more than production-linked incentives to boost manufacturing
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / India needs more than production-linked incentives to boost manufacturingIndia needs more than production-linked incentives to boost manufacturing

Subsidies alone cannot make Indian manufacturing competitive. The assessment makes a clear case for balancing supply-side incentives with demand-side support

premium

Representative Picture

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 16 2026 | 11:16 PM ISTThe production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme, introduced in 2020, was intended to address India’s manufacturing disadvantages, attract investment, reduce import dependence, and improve its position in global supply chains. The first comprehensive assessment of the 14 schemes under the PLI, released last week by the NITI Aayog, in collaboration with the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad, suggests that the scheme has expanded investment and production, but the impact remains uneven. By March 2026, the scheme had cumulatively attracted ₹2.4 trillion in investment and generated production worth ₹22.66 trillion, achieving 76 per cent and 64 per cent of the respective full-tenure targets. Employment generation, however, stood at just 28 per cent of the target of 3.02 million. As noted in this report, this employment gap needs to be viewed in the context of the gestation period of manufacturing investment. Capital expenditure generally takes place before the factories become fully operational, while production and hiring gather pace as capacity utilisation improves. Nevertheless, the translation of investment into sustainable jobs, particularly in labour-intensive industries, needs closer monitoring.  The export performance offers some encouragement. Cumulative exports reported under the PLI schemes increased from ₹4 trillion in 2023-24 to ₹15.2 trillion in 2025-26. Mobile manufacturing has been a notable success, but much of the activity remains concentrated in final assembly, with continued dependence on imported high-value components. The demand for continued incentives and the recently notified Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme underline the need to deepen domestic capabilities by encouraging technology transfer, greater domestic sourcing, and investment in design and research & development. Progress in other sectors has been slow. Under the advanced chemistry cell battery programme, only 1.4 gigawatt-hour (Gwh) of capacity has been developed against the 50 Gwh target, with commercial production yet to begin. By contrast, the experience of the white-goods sector, where domestic value addition increased from 20 per cent to 55 per cent, shows that deeper localisation is possible.  More broadly, the performance of the PLI schemes needs to be assessed against India’s larger manufacturing ambitions. Despite an increase in manufacturing output, the sector’s contribution to the economy has not registered a sustained rise. Under the revised national accounts series, manufacturing’s share in gross value added at current prices was 14.7 per cent in 2022-23, remained unchanged in 2023-24, declined to 14.5 per cent in 2024-25, and recovered marginally to 14.8 per cent in 2025-26. This suggests that expanding production in select sectors has not yet translated into a significant structural shift in the economy.  Subsidies alone cannot make Indian manufacturing competitive. The assessment makes a clear case for balancing supply-side incentives with demand-side support. Stronger market linkages and export-market development can help create a more reliable market for domestic producers. The focus must also be on strengthening micro, small and medium enterprises, which can supply components and intermediate goods to larger manufacturers. Better access to finance, technology upgrade, workforce skilling, and improvement in testing facilities would help them integrate into domestic and global value chains. The incentives can attract factories, but sustained manufacturing growth will depend on making Indian production more competitive. It is also worth highlighting that the scheme should not take policy attention away from broader reforms. Increasing manufacturing output will need policy reforms in areas like land, labour, capital and trade.     Topics : Business Standard Editorial Comment BS Opinion PLI scheme manufacturing

entry.title: Nvidia's dominance and succession risks expose fragility in the AI boom
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Nvidia's dominance and succession risks expose fragility in the AI boomNvidia's dominance and succession risks expose fragility in the AI boom

Nvidia clawed its way up from being a specialist in graphics co-processors to become the dominant player in gaming, and then in AI

premium

Nvidia, which was until recently the most valuable company in the world, provides the most crucial component of the hardware infrastructure underpinning the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 16 2026 | 12:24 AM ISTGlobal stock markets are assessing a situation that management theorists describe as “concentration risk”. The exit of Jensen Huang, who was reportedly honey-trapped, as chief executive officer of Nvidia has created considerable uncertainty about the company’s future. Nvidia, which was until recently the most valuable company in the world, provides the most crucial component of the hardware infrastructure underpinning the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom. More broadly, Nvidia holds a dominant market share across the rest of the information technology (IT) industry, and enjoys monopoly status in graphics-intensive spaces such as gaming. Nvidia did not have a succession plan because Mr Jensen did not believe in one. About 60 departments reported directly to him. This may have worked well to accelerate the pace of strategic decisions. But the lack of a formal succession plan means that the Nvidia board must face the challenges of appointing a capable team. That team must develop and articulate a consistent business strategy, and restore investor confidence in a $4 trillion company. Moreover, Nvidia faces investigations from multiple agencies of the United States (US) government and will likely be forced to answer questions in the US Congress. The leadership vacuum has also led Wall Street to suddenly focus on a possible financial weakness in Nvidia’s circular sales strategy. The chipmaker has an excellent credit rating and deploys that to help customers who need to raise debt to buy its chips. The Nvidia balance sheet discloses that it has over $108 billion in outstanding credit guarantees resulting from this circular strategy. One high-profile deal involves selling chips to Oracle, which has debt guarantees from Nvidia. Oracle will use those chips to set up data centres that OpenAI will run. The concentration risks are, therefore, evident. Nvidia holds a dominant share in critical market segments and, if it stumbles operationally, there would be slowdowns across broad swathes of the digital economy. If, in addition, financial issues arise with its guarantees and the circular model blows up, the sums involved are big enough to trigger a crisis across global financial markets. To use an oft-abused phrase, Nvidia may genuinely be too big to fail. And yet, history is not on its side.  It operates in the most hi-tech hardware segment, and no company has maintained dominance for too long in that segment. In prior cycles, IBM, Intel and AMD dominated the chip landscape. Nvidia clawed its way up from being a specialist in graphics co-processors to become the dominant player in gaming, and then in AI. (A co-processor is a chip that runs number-intensive calculations, leaving the main processor in a computer free to do other things.) Google is using its internally designed TPUs (tensor processing units) and intends to start selling and leasing them out. China, officially deprived of access to Nvidia technology, is said to be developing alternatives. But there will be a gap in the market until such alternatives are available in industrial quantities. If Nvidia cannot put a succession plan in place, deal with investigations, sell the succession plan to investors, and navigate the circular financing situation, the exit of one man could result in a cascade of disastrous consequences. The AI bubble is currently deflating, with Nvidia being one of the triggers. If the bubble pops instead of reverting gradually to rational valuations, it could lead to substantial volatility in financial markets if not a full-blown crisis.   Topics : Artificial intelligence Nvidia industry stock markets Global stock markets Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment Jensen Huang

entry.title: As inflation stays elevated, RBI's Dec repo rate increase appears certain
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / As inflation stays elevated, RBI's Dec repo rate increase appears certainAs inflation stays elevated, RBI's Dec repo rate increase appears certain

The MPC in October had projected the retail-inflation rate at 6 per cent for this quarter and 5.7 per cent for the next

premium

Reserve Bank of India (Photo: Reuters)

Business Standard Editorial Comment4 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 10:09 PM ISTThe data released by the National Statistics Office last week showed that the consumer price index-based inflation rate stood at 6.09 per cent in October, breaching the upper end of the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) tolerance band. The rate was at 5.54 per cent in the previous month. An analysis by this newspaper showed that the rate had increased for 12 straight months after bottoming out at 0.04 per cent in October 2025. In October 2026, the food-inflation rate, at about 9 per cent, was the key driver of the headline rate though the core rate too inched up. Inflation pressure is likely to persist in the coming months. Almost all economists agree that the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the RBI will increase the policy repo rate by another 25 basis points in its December meeting, following a 25-basis point increase in the October meeting to 5.5 per cent.  The MPC in October had projected the retail-inflation rate at 6 per cent for this quarter and 5.7 per cent for the next. The rate was projected at 5.6 per cent for the first quarter of 2027-28. The latest inflation print has pushed the real repo rate into negative territory, making a policy-rate adjustment necessary. The extent of adjustment in the December meeting and later will depend on several factors, such as the inflation projection for next financial year, prospects of second-order effects through higher food prices, and the level of the real policy rate the central bank is willing to maintain at this stage.  An earlier study by RBI economists had estimated the neutral rate — the real policy rate that is neither expansionary nor contractionary— at 1.4-1.9 per cent. It is possible that it has changed. Even assuming that the RBI is comfortable maintaining the real policy rate at 1-1.25 per cent, the repo rate needs to be adjusted by 50-75 basis points, given that the central bank expects the inflation rate to average 5 per cent in 2027-28, according to its latest biannual Monetary Policy Report (October). However, much depends on possible shifts in inflation projections. The monsoon season ended with a rainfall deficit of about 13 per cent as against the long-period average. Given the expected strong El Niño conditions, with adverse implications for rain in winter and lower reservoir levels, agricultural output could also be affected in the rabi season, potentially keeping food prices elevated. However, there is some relief, at least for now, on the external front. There are indications that the United States (US) may not resume the Iran war anytime soon, though US action under President Donald Trump remains unpredictable as ever. For now, prices of crude oil have come down significantly. Although gains for India on inflation will remain limited due to the limited pass-through of higher global prices to retail prices, prospects of a lower current-account deficit will support the currency and reduce its impact on inflation outcomes. Lower oil prices and a selloff in artificial intelligence-related stocks in the US have also brought back foreign portfolio investors. While this development will provide stability to the rupee, the RBI will be well advised to use such opportunities to rebuild its foreign-exchange reserves. Stability on the external front will also allow the RBI to focus on inflation management. While the consensus is that the MPC will increase the repo rate by 25 basis points in the December meeting, it may even consider a 50-basis point rate increase to send a strong message, given that growth is not a concern at the moment.   Topics : Inflation RBI retail inflation CPI Inflation repo rate Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Clean books, thin margins: The new reality of Indian banking
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Clean books, thin margins: The new reality of Indian bankingClean books, thin margins: The new reality of Indian banking

As the rate cycle turns, margins should get some relief, but how banks navigate emerging stress in unsecured personal and gold loans remains to be seen

premium

Representative Image

Tamal Bandyopadhyay7 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 10:53 PM ISTWalk into the treasury floor of any bank today, and you’re certain to hear a sigh of relief among dealers. After nearly touching 7.5 per cent in late October, the 10-year benchmark government bond yield is now consolidating between 7.1 per cent and 7.2 per cent.  Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions: When yields rise, bond values fall, triggering a mark-to-market (MTM) hit on banks' treasury income. The country's largest lender, State Bank of India (SBI), saw its treasury income drop about 20 per cent year-on-year (y-o-y) in the September quarter, weighed down by both the earlier uptick in bond yields and a depreciating rupee.  A recent report by CareEdge Ratings pegs the fall in treasury income across select scheduled commercial banks in the September quarter at 61.6 per cent y-o-y. Private sector banks saw a 65.7 per cent drop, sharper than their public sector peers at 59.4 per cent. As bond yields hardened towards the end of the quarter, banks were forced to book MTM losses—the notional loss recognised when the market value of securities falls below their book value, even if they are not sold—and had fewer opportunities to book trading profits.  Another pain point is the persistent squeeze in low-cost current account and savings account (Casa) deposits. All listed universal banks reported a y-o-y drop in their Casa ratio, barring five. Three of them are in the public sector (Indian Overseas Bank or IOB, Union Bank of India and Indian Bank) and two in the private sector (Federal Bank Ltd and Karnataka Bank Ltd). For a few, the contraction was 4 percentage points or more. Among the five exceptions, only IOB recorded a rise—albeit marginal—on both a y-o-y and quarter-on-quarter (q-o-q) basis.  IDFC FIRST Bank Ltd leads the industry with a Casa ratio of 48.4 per cent, followed by Bank of Maharashtra (46.47 per cent), Central Bank of India (44.65 per cent), IDBI Bank Ltd (43.82 per cent), Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd (41.97 per cent) and IOB (40.71 per cent). No other bank has crossed the 40 per cent mark. Among large lenders, SBI, ICICI Bank Ltd and Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd maintained a Casa ratio of at least 38 per cent each, while Axis Bank Ltd had 36 per cent and HDFC Bank Ltd 31.6 per cent. For some lenders, large inflows of foreign currency non-resident (FCNR-B) deposits swelled the term deposit base and pulled the ratio down.  Another headache for bankers is the continued compression in net interest margin (NIM)—broadly, the spread between a bank's yield on advances and its cost of funds. Large private sector lenders bore the brunt of this squeeze due to elevated deposit costs, intense competition for retail funds, and the thin margins earned on the FCNR-B deposits mobilised in large volumes during the quarter.  HDFC Bank's NIM fell 11 basis points (bps) y-o-y and 10 bps q-o-q to 3.16 per cent in the September quarter, its lowest on record. ICICI Bank's margin dropped 12 bps y-o-y and 18 bps sequentially to 4.18 per cent. Axis Bank saw a sharper contraction—down 37 bps y-o-y and 10 bps q-o-q to 3.36 per cent. SBI bucked the trend: Its domestic NIM rose 11 bps sequentially to 3.11 per cent. At 2.94 per cent, its whole-bank NIM was down 3 bps y-o-y but up 8 bps q-o-q. One bps is a hundredth of a percentage point.  Subdued treasury income is a cyclical phenomenon—it routinely occurs when yields harden. The persistent erosion in Casa and NIM, however, points to deeper structural shifts. A steady slide in Casa reflects a fundamental change in how Indian savers deploy their money, forcing banks to adapt to higher funding costs as competition intensifies.  Yet one metric on bank balance sheets signals a far more profound structural transformation and underscores how the business of banking is evolving. No prizes for guessing: It is the steady, continuous decline in bad assets.  Just one public sector bank (PSB) currently has a net non-performing asset (NPA) ratio above 0.5 per cent, alongside five private sector lenders. These six banks are Bandhan Bank Ltd (92 bps), IndusInd Bank Ltd (83 bps), Karnataka Bank Ltd (74 bps), DCB Bank Ltd (73 bps), Punjab & Sind Bank (61 bps) and Jammu & Kashmir Bank (51 bps).  What’s more, every listed bank reported a y-o-y drop in net NPAs in the September quarter. All but one—IDBI Bank—recorded a reduction both y-o-y and q-o-q. IDBI Bank reported a net NPA ratio of 17 bps, down from 21 bps a year ago, though marginally higher than 16 bps in the June quarter.  Among the mega-lenders, SBI reported a net NPA ratio of 36 bps, HDFC Bank 37 bps, ICICI Bank 30 bps and Axis Bank 35 bps. South Indian Bank Ltd boasted the lowest net NPA ratio in the industry at 9 bps, followed by Bank of Maharashtra (12 bps), Tamilnad Mercantile Bank Ltd and Indian Bank (14 bps each), and IOB (16 bps).  On gross NPAs, only two lenders kept their ratio below 1 per cent—Tamilnad Mercantile Bank (61 bps) and Karur Vysya Bank Ltd (69 bps). Next came RBL Bank Ltd (102 bps), Kotak Mahindra Bank (104 bps), HDFC Bank (111 bps), Axis Bank (116 bps), IOB (119 bps), and ICICI Bank and Yes Bank Ltd (120 bps each). SBI's gross NPA ratio stood at 139 bps, its lowest in more than two decades.  In absolute terms, PSBs' gross NPAs fell 12.9 per cent y-o-y to Rs 2.31 trillion at the end of September, while private banks saw a 6.7 per cent drop to Rs 1.28 trillion. Across all listed banks, gross NPAs contracted by 10.8 per cent.  On the net NPA front, PSBs recorded a 13.3 per cent drop to Rs 44,092 crore, while private banks logged a 7.7 per cent decline to Rs 34,606 crore. Aggregate net NPAs across all listed banks fell 10.9 per cent.  To put this turnaround in perspective, gross NPAs of all scheduled commercial banks in India (including foreign banks and small finance banks) had peaked at Rs 10.36 trillion in the fourth quarter of FY18, with net NPAs at Rs 5.21 trillion. At that peak, PSBs accounted for Rs 8.96 trillion of gross NPAs—a staggering 14.6 per cent ratio—and Rs 4.54 trillion of net NPAs (8 per cent). Private banks' gross NPAs then stood at Rs 1.29 trillion (4.7 per cent) and net NPAs at Rs 64,380 crore (2.4 per cent).  On most operational metrics today, PSBs are outperforming their private sector peers. Their operating profits grew 17.2 per cent y-o-y in the September quarter, compared with 13.5 per cent for private banks. Total operating profit for all listed banks rose 15.4 per cent to Rs 1.81 trillion. SBI led with Rs 34,226 crore in operating profit, followed by HDFC Bank (Rs 29,483 crore), ICICI Bank (Rs 20,576 crore), Bank of Baroda (Rs 11,430 crore) and Axis Bank (Rs 11,083 crore). No other lender crossed the Rs 10,000 crore mark.  After setting aside Rs 27,271 crore in provisions for bad loans (down 9.1 per cent y-o-y, though up 7.2 per cent sequentially), aggregate net profit for all listed banks rose 20.1 per cent y-o-y to Rs 1.16 trillion. PSBs and private banks ran neck-and-neck in profit growth. Three lenders crossed the Rs 10,000 crore net profit mark: SBI (Rs 23,038 crore), HDFC Bank (Rs 19,510 crore) and ICICI Bank (Rs 14,843 crore).  So far, the run has been remarkable. In a rising interest rate cycle, floating rate loans reprice upward faster than deposits, lifting NIMs. That should ease the margin squeeze in the coming quarters. But how banks navigate the emerging stress in unsecured personal loans and gold-collateralised lending, however, remains to be seen. ____________________________________________________________________________________________________ The writer is an author and senior advisor to Jana Small Finance Bank Ltd. His latest book: Roller Coaster: An Affair with Banking. To read his previous columns, log on to www.bankerstrust.in. X: @TamalBandyo        Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: India's carbon credit market needs liquidity and credible price signals
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's carbon credit market needs liquidity and credible price signalsIndia's carbon credit market needs liquidity and credible price signals

The need is to have liquidity and depth in the market

premium

Illustration: Ajaya Kumar Mohanty

Ajay TyagiDiya Shah6 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 10:34 PM ISTIt is good news that the United Kingdom has recognised India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) as a pricing mechanism under its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which takes effect in January next year. The benefit to Indian exporters, however, rests entirely on the carbon price the CCTS produces.  The CCTS, as it exists today, needs much improvement. This column focuses on how to have liquidity and depth in the carbon-trading market so that the scheme throws up the right and credible carbon price.  To begin with, the scheme should ensure that there is sufficient demand for carbon-credit certificates (CCCs) in the market at any given time. All the proposed units in different sectors, as announced under the scheme, should be notified in one go. Apart from building demand, this will improve liquidity in the market. The exclusion of high-emitting sectors such as thermal power, which accounts for roughly 40 per cent of national emission, makes no sense. Further, at present, the scheme sets different targets for greenhouse-gas emission for different units in a sector, based on their past emission levels; the laggards in the past have been given softer targets. This is sure to kill demand, besides being unfair to better-performing units. All this would result in an illiquid market and a weak price, not reflective of the true price. The similar category of units within a sector, based on a criterion like revenue or asset size, should be given the same targets. For instance, the integrated steel plants  of similar production capacity should be given the same targets.More importantly, the targets ought to be ambitious from the very beginning, in line with our emission reduction commitments,  and the MRV (measurement, reporting and verification) framework robust. Going forward, more sectors should be notified under the scheme at the earliest.  Under the scheme, entities performing better than the targets would be entitled to get CCCs, which would be credited in their accounts, free of cost, by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE). Underperforming entities can then purchase the required CCCs in the market from those having them.  On the trading of CCCs, one could perhaps take a leaf out of the highly successful process followed in the stock market, though admittedly CCCs and stocks are different.  Like stock exchanges (SEs), the exchanges on which CCCs would trade (herein after referred to as exchanges) may keep a small window before the start of trading day for call auction to determine the opening price of a CCC. In case there is no participation by entities in the call auction, the previous-day closing price will be the opening price. The closing price will be the volume-adjusted weighted average price (VWAP) derived during the last half an hour of trading in the day. Depending on the level of volatility in trading prices at any given time, the exchanges may prescribe a price band, with the floor and ceiling being a certain percentage of the price. The clearing and settlement mechanism may be through a clearing corporation. There are two suggestions for improving liquidity in the carbon-trading market. The exchanges may introduce a market-making scheme in the first few years of trading. Market makers are financial institutions that simultaneously give “buy” and “sell” quotes to improve liquidity. Of course, they would need to be compensated for the losses incurred by them. SEs have schemes on market making for illiquid stocks, eg stocks for small and medium enterprises. The exchanges could learn from the experience of SEs.  The other suggestion to improve the depth of the market is to introduce derivatives trading for CCCs. The obligated entities could lock in compliance costs by buying futures. Futures prices would give an early signal of where the carbon price is heading. The European Union’s Emissions Trading System (EU-ETS) shows the scale this can reach. Nearly 90 per cent of allowances trade as futures, and about 65 per cent of secondary-market participants are financial players who typically sell the futures that compliance firms buy to protect themselves against rising prices. South Korea offers what happens in the absence of financial players. With financial participants initially excluded, allowance trading stalled for eight months in 2015, and only 0.06 per cent of allocated allowances changed hands in the first year. After state banks were appointed market makers in 2019 and financial intermediaries were admitted, annual traded volumes rose from 5.66 million tonnes in 2015 to 54.72 million tonnes by 2021.  While the market for CCCs may be regulated by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC), the futures market may come under the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) like it does for the derivatives market for commodities. A similar arrangement exists for electricity trading. Electricity futures, launched in July 2025, rest on a clear division of roles. The CERC oversees physical power trading on the exchanges, while Sebi regulates futures settled in cash against those exchange prices. A clearing corporation guarantees every contract and collects margins upfront, and protect against defaults. Within their first year, futures volumes on the National Stock Exchange alone reached roughly half the physical day-ahead market, evidence that hedging demand exists once the infrastructure is in place.  The futures on CCCs should trade on  Sebi-regulated exchanges, and settled against the VWAP prices discovered in the physical market. The overall and participant-specific position limits, as a percentage of the trading volumes in the physical market, would need to be put to ensure that the futures market doesn’t manipulate the physical market.  The CCTS begins on a rather tentative note. The scheme was notified in 2023 but trading is yet to start. It is not a good idea to begin the scheme on a weak footing. Any failure would be seen as a non-serious attempt by the government. Except for the suggestions relating to the derivatives market, all other suggestions made above, including allowing financial institutions participation as market makers, may be made part of the scheme right away. The derivatives market may be introduced later at an appropriate time, but the intention to develop it in future should find mention in the scheme now itself so as to give the right message to the world at large about our commitment to develop a credible carbon market in the country. 
The writers are, respectively, former chairman, Sebi, and research assistant, Observer Research Foundation   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Consumer Protection: Insured should not sign away right to full claim
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Consumer Protection: Insured should not sign away right to full claimConsumer Protection: Insured should not sign away right to full claim

The National Commission has held that insistence on a full and final discharge is not justified, as it deprives the insured of their right to take legal action for the balance claim

premium

Policyholders should not sign full and final discharge vouchers if they intend to pursue the balance of their insurance claims.

Jehangir B Gai3 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 10:18 PM ISTLosses suffered by a business can have devastating consequences, not only for the insured but also for its employees and others connected with it. If a business ceases to function, its employees lose their livelihood, while creditors find it challenging to recover the value of goods supplied on credit. Meanwhile, interest and other fixed expenses keep rising, resulting in a crushing financial burden on the insured.  The very purpose of insurance is to insulate a business and safeguard it against unexpected losses. This can happen only if the insurer promptly assesses and settles the claim. Unfortunately, the sad reality is that insurers generally keep claims pending for months. Even when the insurer assesses a claim, it makes several deductions that may or may not be acceptable to the insured.  In cases where the insurer does not pay the full claim, it invariably insists on a full and final discharge before releasing the amount offered. The insured, meanwhile, wants to accept the settlement conditionally, without prejudice to his right to claim the remaining amount that the insurer has disallowed. However, insurers usually capitalise on the insured’s financial predicament and refuse to release the assessed amount, so that they obtain a full and final discharge and the insured forfeits his right to claim the balance. In this column, I will deal with the rights of an insured who finds himself in such a situation.  What does the law say?   The law is well settled that once the insured executes a full and final discharge voucher, he would ordinarily not have the right to claim the balance amount, as the Supreme Court of India held in New India Assurance Co v Genus Power Infrastructure.  An exception to this general rule is permissible only if the insured can establish that he executed the discharge voucher due to coercion, as the Supreme Court of India  laid down in United India Insurance v Ajmer Singh Cotton & General Mills & Ors. Here, the court emphasised that executing discharge vouchers does not inherently prevent policyholders from seeking additional compensation if they can demonstrate that the insurer obtained the vouchers through fraudulent means or undue influence. However, the burden of proof is on the insured, and it is not easy to establish coercion.  The viable remedy  The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) has held that such insistence on a full and final discharge is not justified, as it deprives the insured of their right to take legal action for the balance claim. It held that when the insured gives a discharge “under protest”, the insurer must pay the admitted amount, and withholding it would constitute an unfair trade practice. Hence, in K L Malhotra v Oriental Insurance Co Ltd & Anr and Abhay Neelawarne v New India Assurance Co Ltd & Anr, it issued general directions to stop such unfair practices and ordered the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Irdai) to issue appropriate instructions.  What should the insured do?  An insured must refuse to execute a full and final discharge if he wants to take legal action to recover the balance claim amount. The remedy lies in filing a consumer complaint and applying for interim relief directing the insurer to release the admitted amount.  The writer is a consumer activist     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: The business case for women entrepreneurs: Unlocking credit potential
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The business case for women entrepreneurs: Unlocking credit potentialThe business case for women entrepreneurs: Unlocking credit potential

Women borrowers are emerging as a key growth driver for lenders, offering higher credit growth, lower delinquencies and significant untapped business potential

premium

India’s next phase of credit growth hinges on how effectively lenders serve women entrepreneurs by designing products for them

Manish Shah4 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 9:24 PM ISTFor decades, access to formal credit has been a powerful engine of economic mobility. In India, one of the most significant developments in the credit ecosystem is the growing presence of women borrowers. What began as a financial inclusion effort has steadily evolved into a compelling economic opportunity for financial institutions.  Women borrowers have over the past five years grown at a compound annual growth rate of 14.2 per cent (compared to 8.2 per cent for men), reaching 89 million by December 2025 and accounting for nearly 28 per cent of the retail credit base, according to CRIF High Mark's March 2026 report called The Credit Goes to Her. Their credit portfolios are expanding faster, with 23.4 per cent year-on-year growth (16.7 per cent for men), while active loans are growing more than twice as fast. This positions women as key drivers of incremental credit demand. Women exhibit lower delinquency rates at 2.8 per cent (3.3 per cent for men). Their role in productive credit is also rising steadily, with secured business loans to women growing over 61 per cent year-on-year and accounting for more than half of loan volumes. Women are also the fastest-growing segment of first-time borrowers, with their share in new-to-credit originations increasing from 33 per cent to 41 per cent in two years.  These trends make a compelling case: Women borrowers offer higher growth, lower risk and long-term value, making them central to the future of lending. The rise of the woman entrepreneur is seen from neighbourhood retail outlets and service businesses to emerging digital ventures. Across sectors and geographies, more women are moving beyond participation and becoming key economic contributors and business decision-makers. This shift is particularly visible in smaller cities and emerging markets, where access to formal finance is enabling women entrepreneurs to scale businesses, generate employment and contribute meaningfully to local economies.  Despite encouraging progress, several structural challenges continue to shape women’s access to credit. Collateral ownership remains limited, with many women lacking formal property titles required for secured lending. Financial awareness and confidence gaps also continue to influence borrowing behaviour, particularly in smaller markets. In addition, digital access gaps persist across certain borrower segments, even as digital lending platforms expand rapidly.  Encouragingly, government initiatives have helped address some of these barriers. Programmes such as the Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana have enabled millions of women to access formal credit. Institutional support has also strengthened women-led self-help group networks, helping connect rural borrowers to the formal banking system. These developments reinforce an important principle: When women gain access to formal finance, they use it productively and repay it responsibly.  A critical gap persists between social-sector lending and mainstream commercial finance for women. While microfinance and self-help groups have enabled access to small-ticket credit, many women entrepreneurs struggle to transition into larger, formal lending ecosystems. This creates a “missing middle”, where businesses are too large for microfinance yet not adequately served by traditional banking. As a result, women-led enterprises continue to face a significant financing gap, estimated to be as high as 70 per cent, representing a large untapped opportunity for formal financial institutions.  Bridging this gap will require a shift in how lenders assess and serve women borrowers. Despite demonstrating strong repayment behaviour, women often receive smaller loan sizes and limited access to growth capital. Addressing this calls for more inclusive underwriting models, greater use of alternative data and stronger support systems.  For lenders, the path forward is clear. Women borrowers represent a high-quality credit segment that remains underserved relative to its potential. Financial institutions that invest early in this segment will not only support economic inclusion but also strengthen their own business fundamentals. Designing products tailored for women entrepreneurs, building advisory support mechanisms and expanding outreach can unlock long-term value.  In many ways, the next phase of credit growth will be shaped by how effectively the financial ecosystem engages with women entrepreneurs.

entry.title: Scotch at the docks tests India-UK trade arrangement's tariff concessions
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Scotch at the docks tests India-UK trade arrangement's tariff concessionsScotch at the docks tests India-UK trade arrangement's tariff concessions

The India-UK trade pact offers lower duties on eligible Scotch whisky imports, but the applicable tariff depends on the classification of goods under the Customs Tariff and exemption notification

premium

The India-UK trade agreement envisages an initial duty of 75 per cent on imports of eligible Scotch whisky, with the rate falling to 40 per cent over 10 years

TNC Rajagopalan3 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 6:18 PM ISTLast week, Reuters reported that several consignments of Scotch whisky imported from the United Kingdom (UK) were held up at the ports. The importers seek clearance at 75 per cent Customs duty under the India-UK trade agreement, whereas the Customs seek duty at 150 per cent. On Friday, the Commerce Secretary said that the Ministry of Finance had engaged with the stakeholders and that India would honour the duty concessions under the agreement.  The India-UK trade agreement envisages an initial duty of 75 per cent on imports of eligible Scotch whisky, with the rate falling to 40 per cent over 10 years. Entries at serial numbers 827 and 830 of Table I to notification No. 29/2026-Cus dated July 14, 2026, give effect to the initial concession. Both entries say “All goods” against tariff items 22083012 and 22083092 and prescribe 25 per cent basic Customs duty (BCD) and 50 per cent Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess (AIDC), subject to the conditions in the notification, including those relating to origin.  The case of the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) appears to be that the items imported are concentrates or compound alcoholic preparations of a kind used for the manufacture of beverages. According to Reuters, the DRI, in a memo dated November 4, asked the Customs field formations  to apply the higher rate to such goods. The investigators reportedly take the view that the concession applies to finished products such as bottled Scotch. The distinction to be made is between whisky as imported and an alcoholic preparation used to make a beverage. UK verification guidance recognises that Scotch whisky can be shipped in bulk at high strength and diluted before bottling.  In October, India and the UK cited Scotch whisky as an early success of their trade agreement. Their October 12 joint statement said it had already entered India at reduced tariffs, without giving particulars of the goods cleared. Incidentally, tariff item 21069051 entered the Customs Tariff on May 1, 2026, through the Finance Act, 2026, when tariff item 21069050 was split into 21069051 and 21069059. The new item for compound alcoholic preparations carries 150 per cent BCD. The July notification gives no concession against that entry.  Interestingly, the DGFT’s ITC (HS) import schedule gives the description against 22083092 as Scotch in containers holding more than two litres. The Customs Tariff gives the description “Scotch” against both 22083012 and 22083092 under the six-digit subheading 220830 for whiskies. The first item comes under “In containers holding 2 litres or less” and the second under “Other”. The word "Other" must be read at the same level as the preceding description relating to container size.  So, Scotch whisky in containers holding more than two litres gets the same concession as Scotch whisky in smaller containers. If, however, the goods as imported answer to the description of compound alcoholic preparations under tariff item 21069051, Customs would be on firmer ground in denying the exemption.  Importers should, therefore, go by the actual wording of the exemption notification issued by the Ministry of Finance, read with the Customs tariff. The text of the trade agreement, government press releases and reports in the media may help them understand the concession but importers should satisfy themselves that the  imported  goods answer to the tariff description and meet the conditions of the exemption notification.     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer.
